title: The Girl Who Counted Crows
summary: The crows of Blackfen carry away the secrets people whisper, and no one dares count them. When Junia counts the whole murder to learn one buried secret, she opens a door she was never meant to open — and learns some things are hidden to protect the people who hid them.

chapters.title: The Keepers of Whispers
chapters.body:
In Blackfen, when you had a secret too heavy to hold, you gave it to the crows.

You went out to the old dead oak at the edge of the marsh at dusk, where the crows gathered black and countless in the bare branches, and you whispered your secret up into them — the thing you'd done and couldn't undo, the truth you couldn't say aloud, the grief you couldn't carry. And a crow would tilt its head, and listen, and take your secret up into the sky, and carry it away. You'd walk home lighter. The crows kept the secrets of Blackfen, all of them, going back further than anyone could remember. Nobody knew where they took them. Nobody asked.

And there was one rule, the oldest rule in Blackfen, that everyone obeyed without knowing why: you never, ever counted the crows.

Junia was thirteen and full of a particular kind of stubbornness — the kind that hears "you must never" and immediately wants to know why not. She'd asked, of course. She'd asked her mother, her teacher, the old marsh-warden. They'd all given her the same uneasy non-answer: you just don't, child. It's not done. Leave the crows uncounted. And every non-answer only made the wanting-to-know burn brighter.

But it wasn't idle curiosity that finally drove her to it. It was her brother.

A year ago, Junia's older brother Ash had gone out to the dead oak at dusk, whispered something up into the crows, and walked into the marsh and never come back. They'd found his coat, but not him. And no one would tell Junia what he'd whispered — whether anyone even knew — or why a boy who'd seemed happy that morning would give the crows a secret and then walk into the fen. The not-knowing ate at her. Somewhere in those black uncountable birds was her brother's last secret, the one that might explain why. And she wanted it back.

So she went to the marsh-warden, old Coll, and asked him straight: "How do I get a secret back from the crows?"

Coll went very still. "You don't," he said. "What's given is given."

"But there must be a way," Junia pressed. "The rule says don't count them. Rules like that only exist because the thing they forbid does something. So — what does counting them do?"

The old warden looked at her for a long, long moment, and then, because he was tired and old and could see she wouldn't let it go, he told her.

"If you count the whole murder," he said quietly, "every crow, to the last one, without losing your place — then the crows must give up what they carry. All of it. Every secret they hold comes back down at once, to the one who counted." He leaned close, and his voice dropped. "But hear me, girl. There's a reason no one does it. The crows don't just carry your secrets. They carry everyone's. Every secret ever given to them, all the way back. And most secrets are hidden for a reason. You count those birds, and you won't get back one secret. You'll get back all of them. And some things are buried to protect the living. You don't want to dig up a whole marsh of buried things to find one bone."

But Junia had already decided. Her brother's secret was in those birds. And she would count every last crow to get it back.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.body:
Junia went to the dead oak at dusk, when the crows came home to roost, and she began to count.

One. Two. Three. They settled black into the bare branches, hundreds of them, more than hundreds, and she counted them steadily under her breath, pointing with her eyes, holding her place with fierce concentration. Ten. Eleven. Twelve. The crows noticed. They always know when they're being counted — it's why the rule exists — and one by one their black heads turned toward her, their eyes bright and knowing, and the marsh went quiet around her the way it had gone quiet for a hundred years whenever someone was foolish enough to try.

Forty. Forty-one. It was harder than she'd thought. The crows shifted and hopped, trying to make her lose her place, and the light was failing, and her eyes ached. But Junia was stubborn to her bones. Ninety. Ninety-one. Two hundred. Two hundred and six. She counted on, and on, as the dusk deepened to dark and the stars came out over the marsh, and still the crows came, and still she counted, refusing to lose the thread.

And as she neared the end — as she counted the last of the great black murder, the final few crows in the highest branches — she began to feel them. The secrets. Pressing at the edges of the count, straining against the birds that held them, a hundred years of Blackfen's buried truths crowding to come down. She could feel their weight. Their number. The sheer terrible mass of everything the town had ever wanted to forget.

"Four hundred and eleven," she whispered. "Four hundred and twelve."

One crow left. The last one, alone on the highest bare twig, watching her with its bright black eye.

Junia hesitated. Old Coll's warning was loud in her head now — some things are buried to protect the living. But her brother's secret was up there. She had come this far. She counted the last crow.

"Four hundred and thirteen."

And the sky broke open.

Every crow rose at once, a great roaring black cloud, and from them poured down a hundred years of secrets — not as birds, but as voices, whispers, a deluge of them falling on Junia all at once. She had wanted one secret. She got all of them.

And it was unbearable. She heard the baker's secret, that the fire that killed his brother was his own careless fault. She heard her teacher's secret, a love she'd hidden her whole life in shame. She heard secrets of theft and cowardice and old cruelties, secrets of who had betrayed whom, whose child belonged to whom, which kind old neighbor had once done a terrible thing. The whole hidden underside of Blackfen poured into her at once — every wound the town had given the crows to carry so it wouldn't have to look at them. And Junia understood, drowning in it, exactly what Coll had meant. These secrets weren't hidden out of mere shame. They were hidden because knowing them would break things. Would turn neighbor against neighbor. Would reopen wounds a whole town had spent a hundred years letting scar over.

And somewhere in the flood, she found it. Her brother's voice. Ash's last secret, the one she'd counted four hundred and thirteen crows to hear.

chapters.title: What Was Buried to Protect
chapters.body:
Her brother's secret was small, and quiet, and it broke Junia's heart in a way she had not expected.

Ash had not walked into the marsh in despair over some dark thing. His secret was this: he had been sick. Quietly, for months, with something growing in him that the healers couldn't name or stop, and he had known he was dying, and he had not wanted his family to watch him waste away. So he had whispered his sickness to the crows — given away the secret of it, the fear of it, the weight of it — and then he had walked into the marsh on his own terms, while he was still himself, sparing the people he loved the long horror of watching him go. He'd left his coat so they'd know he was gone. He'd taken the rest of the truth to the crows so they'd never have to carry the knowing.

He had hidden it to protect them.

Junia knelt in the marsh grass under the roaring sky, her brother's last secret in her hands at last, and wept — not only for him, but for what she finally understood. Some things are buried to protect the people who bury them. Ash hadn't hidden his death because he was ashamed. He'd hidden it as a gift — the last gift he could give, a mercy, a shield held over the people he loved. And she had just torn that gift open. Worse: she had torn open everyone's. A whole town's worth of mercies and shields and carefully scarred-over wounds, all raining down on her at once, ready to poison Blackfen the moment she carried them home and let them loose.

Because that was the danger now. She held all of it. Every secret. And if she walked back into town knowing what she knew — the baker's guilt, the teacher's shame, the betrayals, the buried cruelties — she could not un-know them. They would leak out of her, in a look, in a word, in the way she couldn't meet someone's eyes. She would become a walking wound in the side of a town that had spent a century healing. She had wanted one truth. She'd stolen a hundred, and most of them were not hers to carry, and knowing them would help no one and hurt everyone.

And Junia understood the last, hardest thing. Getting the secrets back was not the victory. Knowing them was the curse. The crows had been a mercy all along — not hiding the truth from Blackfen, but carrying it for Blackfen, so that people could live alongside their worst moments without being crushed by them or turned against each other by them. She had mistaken the crows for thieves of truth. They were its keepers. Its protectors. The reason the town could go on.

So Junia did the only thing she could. She stood up in the roaring dark, and she lifted her face to the great black cloud of crows still wheeling overhead, and she gave the secrets back.

One by one — the baker's fire, the teacher's love, the betrayals, the cruelties, all of them — she whispered each secret back up into the sky, returning it to the crows, unburdening herself of the knowing. It took all night. It was the hardest thing she'd ever done, harder than the counting, because each secret she gave back she had to first hold, and understand, and then choose not to keep — choose not to be the person who knew. She gave back the baker's guilt so the baker could keep living. She gave back the teacher's shame so the teacher could keep her dignity. She gave every stolen mercy back to the birds that had guarded it.

And last of all, she came to her brother's secret. And this one she almost kept — because it was hers, because it was Ash, because knowing why he'd gone was a thing she'd wanted for a year. But she understood, now, that he had given it away on purpose, as a kindness, and that the kindest thing she could do in return was honor the gift. Not to hide the truth from herself out of fear — she would always know, now, that he had died protecting them, and that knowing was a gift too. But the weight of it, the crushing fear-soaked weight of his slow dying, the part he'd wanted no one to carry — that she gave back to the crows, so that she could remember him with love instead of horror.

"Thank you," she whispered to him, up into the black wings. "For protecting us. I understand now. I'll carry that you loved us. Let the crows carry the rest."

And she gave the last of it back, and the sky quieted, and the crows settled once more into the dead oak, uncounted, keeping their hundred years of mercies safe.

Junia walked home in the dawn light, empty-handed and full-hearted. She never told anyone what she'd learned, because she'd learned it wasn't hers to tell — that was the whole point. She knew the baker's kind eyes hid a guilt, and she smiled at him the same as ever, and let him keep his peace. She knew a hundred hidden things about Blackfen, in the shape of having once known them, and she let every one of them stay buried, because she finally understood that some truths are hidden not out of lies, but out of love.

And on dusks after that, when she saw someone walk out to the dead oak to whisper their weight up into the waiting birds, Junia no longer wondered what they carried, or where the crows took it. She just watched the black wings lift the secret into the dark, and was glad — glad there was somewhere to put the things too heavy to hold, and glad, most of all, that she had learned to leave the crows uncounted.
